Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.

Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.

ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local

local revenue.32

block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”

At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)

So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.
A YES VOTE ON PROPOSITION 43 A NO VOTE ON PROPOSITION 43

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

# No.

## What Prop 43 actually does

Prop 43 would amend the California Constitution so that local "special taxes" (taxes earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by **citizen initiative** must get **two-thirds approval**, instead of the current simple majority — starting January 1, 2027. Taxes proposed by city councils/boards already need two-thirds; the courts (in the *Upland* case and follow-ups from 2017–2024) held that citizen-initiated versions need only a majority. It's prospective only — nothing already passed gets revoked.

## Why I land on No

1. **Minority rule.** This is the core problem. Under Prop 43, just 33.4% of voters can block a measure that 66.6% of their neighbors support. A supermajority check made sense as a constraint on *government* imposing taxes. But when the people themselves gather signatures and then vote to tax themselves at the ballot box, majority rule is the more democratic standard. The courts' reasoning — that the initiative power "coexists with, not displaces" Prop 218's restrictions — is sound.

2. **Real measures, real services would have failed.** Under the 2/3 threshold, these majority-passed citizen initiatives would never have become law: Sonoma County's wildfire/emergency-services sales tax (62%), SF's childcare tax (51%) and homeless-services tax (61%), Fresno's parks tax (52%), and LA's Measure ULA housing/homelessness tax (58%). Firefighters, teachers, nurses, the League of Women Voters, and the State PTA all oppose it — and all taxes of *special districts* (fire, hospital, library districts) are classified as special taxes, so those communities lose the most.

3. **It doesn't cut a single tax.** It just removes a funding tool while providing zero relief — and the fiscal timing is bad, with local budgets squeezed by inflation and federal health/human-services cuts.

4. **It's a hostage artifact.** Prop 43 exists only as the ransom paid to withdraw the Howard Jarvis initiative that would have *retroactively* voided taxes like LA's mansion tax. That initiative is already off the ballot — so a Yes vote buys you nothing from that deal. Even its own author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, is "adamantly opposed" to it, and Gov. Newsom, the Sac Bee, LA Times, and the state Democratic Party all urge No.

**The honest case for Yes:** if you believe taxation requires broad consensus, want parity between government- and citizen-proposed special taxes, and distrust the "council allies run it as an initiative to dodge 2/3" maneuvering, the Yes side is coherent. The Chronicle even declined to oppose it for that reason. But on the merits — democracy and practical local-services impact — **vote No**.

**Decision framework:**

4. The measure's origin: authored by someone adamantly opposed to it; it was the ransom to remove a much worse retroactive initiative. That initiative is already off the ballot, so voting YES on 43 gains nothing beyond the threshold change itself.

5. It does not reduce anyone's current taxes; it only restricts future revenue-raising tools.

# No.

## What Prop 43 actually does

Prop 43 would amend the California Constitution so that local "special taxes" (taxes earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by **citizen initiative** must get **two-thirds approval**, instead of the current simple majority — starting January 1, 2027. Taxes proposed by city councils/boards already need two-thirds; the courts (in the *Upland* case and follow-ups from 2017–2024) held that citizen-initiated versions need only a majority. It's prospective only — nothing already passed gets revoked.

## Why I land on No

1. **Minority rule.** This is the core problem. Under Prop 43, just 33.4% of voters can block a measure that 66.6% of their neighbors support. A supermajority check made sense as a constraint on *government* imposing taxes. But when the people themselves gather signatures and then vote to tax themselves at the ballot box, majority rule is the more democratic standard. The courts' reasoning — that the initiative power "coexists with, not displaces" Prop 218's restrictions — is sound.

2. **Real measures, real services would have failed.** Under the 2/3 threshold, these majority-passed citizen initiatives would never have become law: Sonoma County's wildfire/emergency-services sales tax (62%), SF's childcare tax (51%) and homeless-services tax (61%), Fresno's parks tax (52%), and LA's Measure ULA housing/homelessness tax (58%). Firefighters, teachers, nurses, the League of Women Voters, and the State PTA all oppose it — and all taxes of *special districts* (fire, hospital, library districts) are classified as special taxes, so those communities lose the most.

3. **It doesn't cut a single tax.** It just removes a funding tool while providing zero relief — and the fiscal timing is bad, with local budgets squeezed by inflation and federal health/human-services cuts.

4. **It's a hostage artifact.** Prop 43 exists only as the ransom paid to withdraw the Howard Jarvis initiative that would have *retroactively* voided taxes like LA's mansion tax. That initiative is already off the ballot — so a Yes vote buys you nothing from that deal. Even its own author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, is "adamantly opposed" to it, and Gov. Newsom, the Sac Bee, LA Times, and the state Democratic Party all urge No.

**The honest case for Yes:** if you believe taxation requires broad consensus, want parity between government- and citizen-proposed special taxes, and distrust the "council allies run it as an initiative to dodge 2/3" maneuvering, the Yes side is coherent. The Chronicle even declined to oppose it for that reason. But on the merits — democracy and practical local-services impact — **vote No**.

Key background:
- Prop 13 (1978) required two-thirds for local special taxes imposed by governments
- Prop 218 (1996) reaffirmed two-thirds for special taxes placed by governments
- California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017) suggested citizen-initiated taxes might be treated differently

- Prop 43 arose from a compromise: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association had an initiative (1983) that would have required two-thirds for ALL local tax measures (including government-proposed general taxes), which was withdrawn in exchange for the legislature placing ACA 22 (Prop 43) on the ballot
- Prop 43 only affects citizen-initiated special taxes going forward, prospectively from January 1, 2027
- It stems from the LA "mansion tax" fight (Measure ULA) — which was a citizen initiative passed with 57% majority vote in March 2022

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.
PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.
Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.
PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.
Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.
PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.
KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS-WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.
That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Nick Lapis , Director of Advocacy
Californians Against Waste
Bill Barnes , Director of Campaigns & Community
Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California
Steve Frisch , President
Sierra Business Council
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.
Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out-or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods-that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare-especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote-and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge-even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away-to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.
That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO on Prop. 43:
• California Professional Firefighters • Californians Against Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California School Employees Association • Communities for a Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of SEIU California • Sierra Business Council
Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs-with you and your neighbors.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Harkins , Executive Director
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects- then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved-preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.
Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Greg Van Dyke , Chairman
California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and
Safety

The CalMatters logo. CalMatters is a nonpartisan and nonprofit news organization covering California (CalMatters via Bay City News)

CalMatters
In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services.
Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43, which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services.
Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups.
Californians voted in 1996 to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes -- until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify. Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority.
Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow "minority rule" because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes.
Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money.
"The power to tax is (the) government's most draconian power," he told CalMatters. "The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus."
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted.
"Under Prop. 43, it's clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else," he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal.
Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California.
PROP. 43 ORIGINATED FROM L.A.'S 'MANSION TAX' FIGHT
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles' "mansion tax," a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city.
The tax angered real estate developers and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal's group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax.
Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language. The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax.
Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is "adamantly opposed" to it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
"The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy," Wicks said in a social media post.
IS THERE PUBLIC APPETITE?
This isn't Coupal's first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state's constitution.
How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A September survey from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes.
But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters' concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California.
"We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed," he said. "California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more."
