Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.
table of contents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
Glossary of Key Terms
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Examples of enterprise districts include health care districts, airport districts, water districts, and other utility districts. Non-enterprise districts provide benefits to entire communities — such as fire protection and road repair services — and are primarily funded by property taxes and other types of taxes and assessments. As noted above, taxes levied by special districts are always considered special taxes so they require approval of two-thirds of voters in the district, unless they are placed on the ballot by voters.
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Would Make It More Difficult for Communities to Generate Revenues to Meet Local Needs
California already imposes high barriers to raising local revenues by requiring all special taxes levied by local governments to be approved by two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority, and by classifying certain types of taxes — parcel taxes and taxes levied by special districts and school districts — as special taxes subject to higher vote requirements. Extending the two-thirds vote requirement to voter-initiated special tax proposals, as Prop. 43 proposes, would decrease the likelihood that these measures would pass, even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure and the services that the new revenues would fund.
In contrast to the high bar for raising taxes, local governments do not need voter approval to reduce services — and cuts to services often result when localities face revenue shortfalls. Yet, communities also have the option of raising revenues to help close budget gaps. If Prop. 43 passes, counties and cities would still have the ability to raise general taxes with approval from a simple majority of voters to shore up local services. Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

content.thinking:
I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me compile my research and give a clear answer.

Summary of research:

**What Prop 43 does:** Constitutional amendment (legislative, ACA 22 by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks) requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote for local special taxes proposed by citizen initiative, starting January 1, 2027. Currently, special taxes proposed by local government bodies require two-thirds, but citizen-initiated special taxes can pass with a simple majority (per court decisions since 2017: Upland (2017), City and County of SF v. All Persons re: Prop C (2020), Fresno Building Healthy Communities (2020), Alameda County (2024), which the CA Supreme Court declined to review). Prospective only — doesn't touch taxes already approved.

**Backstory:** Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association + California Business Roundtable qualified a much more sweeping, retroactive initiative (#1983, "Local Taxpayer Protection Act") for the 2026 ballot that would have invalidated previously passed majority-vote taxes like LA's Measure ULA ("mansion tax," 58% in 2022, $1.4B raised since 2023) and capped transfer taxes. To kill that, Newsom/Wicks/legislative leaders struck a deal: the initiative was withdrawn, the legislature's counter-measure ACA 13 was withdrawn, and ACA 22 (the narrower Prop 43) was placed on the ballot instead. Wicks herself says she's "adamantly opposed" to it — she authored it purely as a bargaining chip. Passed nearly unanimously in the legislature because it was the only path to kill the worse retroactive measure.

**Who's on which side:**
- YES: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, CalTaxpayers Assn, CA Business Roundtable (~$15M, ~$10M from CA Business Roundtable PAC), Family Business Assn, CA Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, CA Small Business Assn, Reform California, CA Republican Party.
- NO: CA Professional Firefighters, CA Federation of Teachers, CTA, Nurse Alliance of SEIU, CSEA, League of Women Voters, CA Democratic Party, State PTA, League of California Cities, CSAC, Newsom, affordable housing groups, labor. ~$6M.

**Impacts:**
- LAO: fiscal impact unknown; possibility that local revenues will not rise as much.
- Examples of majority-passed citizen-initiated special taxes that would have failed under 2/3: SF Prop C (childcare, 51% in 2018), Fresno Measure P (parks, 52%), LA Measure ULA (housing/homelessness, 58%), Sonoma County (wildfire/emergency services, 62% in 2024), SF Prop C homeless services (61% 2018), Madera County Measure T (transportation, 52%).
- All special districts' taxes (fire, hospital, transit, library districts) are "special taxes" by definition, so citizen-initiated tax measures for them would face the higher bar regardless of earmarking.
- The measure also technically re-states the prohibition on ad valorem property taxes except as authorized.

**Arguments YES:** Restores Prop 13's intent; equal standard for all special taxes; taxes = government's coercive power, need broad consensus; prevents strategic end-runs where officials collaborate with unions/advocates to run taxes as "citizen initiatives" to dodge the 2/3 rule; CA is already heavily taxed; protects homeowners from high transfer taxes; prospective only.

**Arguments NO:** Minority rule (33.4% can block what 66.6% want); makes it much harder to fund fire/911, schools, parks, libraries, housing, especially amid federal cuts (H.R.1) and wildfire risk; doesn't cut taxes at all, just removes a funding tool; the courts' reading (initiative power coexists with, not displaced by, Prop 218 restrictions) is legitimate — when a majority of voters themselves vote to tax themselves, that IS voter approval; entrenches CA's already incoherent tax structure; authored by someone who opposes it; originally the price of killing a worse measure, so a YES isn't even needed now to keep the Jarvis initiative off the ballot (it's already withdrawn).

**Polls:** PPIC Oct: 42 yes/55 no; Berkeley IGS Oct: 36/46/18. Forecast: likely to fail (~3% chance).

**Editorials:** Sac Bee + McClatchy papers: NO. LA Times (Skelton): No ("undemocratic"). SF Chronicle: no formal position — sympathizes with parts but says it's not a solution. Newsom: No.

**Decision framework:**
The user asks for a yes or no. Weighing:

1. Democratic principle: Two-thirds vote requirements allow a minority to veto majority-supported measures. For taxes proposed by the people themselves via initiative, majority rule is more defensible than for taxes imposed by a government body — the check on government power rationale doesn't apply. The courts agreed.

2. Practical impact: Forecloses a pathway used for popular measures — wildfire response (Sonoma 62%), childcare (SF 51%), parks (Fresno 52%), homelessness/housing (LA 58%, SF 61%). Revenues are already strained by Prop 13-era constraints and federal cuts. CalBudget Center: would make it harder for communities to meet needs.

3. Strategic behavior concern is real (councils dodging the 2/3 rule via ally-run initiatives) but that's a smaller harm than the minority-veto problem, and governments still have the general-tax majority route; the measure doesn't address the underlying fiscal structure (Chronicle's point: it "cements a broken system" either way).

4. The measure's origin: authored by someone adamantly opposed to it; it was the ransom to remove a much worse retroactive initiative. That initiative is already off the ballot, so voting YES on 43 gains nothing beyond the threshold change itself.

5. It does not reduce anyone's current taxes; it only restricts future revenue-raising tools.

On balance: NO.

# No.

## What Prop 43 actually does

Prop 43 would amend the California Constitution so that local "special taxes" (taxes earmarked for a specific purpose) proposed by **citizen initiative** must get **two-thirds approval**, instead of the current simple majority — starting January 1, 2027. Taxes proposed by city councils/boards already need two-thirds; the courts (in the *Upland* case and follow-ups from 2017–2024) held that citizen-initiated versions need only a majority. It's prospective only — nothing already passed gets revoked.

## Why I land on No

1. **Minority rule.** This is the core problem. Under Prop 43, just 33.4% of voters can block a measure that 66.6% of their neighbors support. A supermajority check made sense as a constraint on *government* imposing taxes. But when the people themselves gather signatures and then vote to tax themselves at the ballot box, majority rule is the more democratic standard. The courts' reasoning — that the initiative power "coexists with, not displaces" Prop 218's restrictions — is sound.

2. **Real measures, real services would have failed.** Under the 2/3 threshold, these majority-passed citizen initiatives would never have become law: Sonoma County's wildfire/emergency-services sales tax (62%), SF's childcare tax (51%) and homeless-services tax (61%), Fresno's parks tax (52%), and LA's Measure ULA housing/homelessness tax (58%). Firefighters, teachers, nurses, the League of Women Voters, and the State PTA all oppose it — and all taxes of *special districts* (fire, hospital, library districts) are classified as special taxes, so those communities lose the most.

3. **It doesn't cut a single tax.** It just removes a funding tool while providing zero relief — and the fiscal timing is bad, with local budgets squeezed by inflation and federal health/human-services cuts.

4. **It's a hostage artifact.** Prop 43 exists only as the ransom paid to withdraw the Howard Jarvis initiative that would have *retroactively* voided taxes like LA's mansion tax. That initiative is already off the ballot — so a Yes vote buys you nothing from that deal. Even its own author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, is "adamantly opposed" to it, and Gov. Newsom, the Sac Bee, LA Times, and the state Democratic Party all urge No.

**The honest case for Yes:** if you believe taxation requires broad consensus, want parity between government- and citizen-proposed special taxes, and distrust the "council allies run it as an initiative to dodge 2/3" maneuvering, the Yes side is coherent. The Chronicle even declined to oppose it for that reason. But on the merits — democracy and practical local-services impact — **vote No**.
